A similar change from the Kogen team has landed separately and has its own screen, so this candidate is dropped, not stacked.

findings.title: Build changes remain unverified after an incomplete screen
findings.summary: Five of nine assigned attempts ran: three stopped while shaping the specification and two stopped on protected acceptance contradictions. None landed or reached review, so this screen leaves the build changes unresolved and does not qualify them for adoption. Four assignments stayed unrun under capacity and delivery-priority gates. The source reconstruction patch and all observed outcomes are published; missing outcomes remain unknown.

findings.title: Executor policy move cannot compile in the adopted assembly
findings.summary: Moving phase policy out of executor needs compatible consumers. The frozen candidate assembly failed before any model run, so behaviour remains unresolved.

findings.title: Loop output line boundaries need a triggered confirmation
findings.summary: A three-task smoke screen checks a loop update that preserves complete lines in long tool output. Targeted contracts pass and fake-provider replay identifies the exact request-byte change. The logging prefix is unchanged toward the model; the changed output path needs a live trigger before adoption.

findings.title: Verification timeout diagnostics remain unconfirmed in task runs
findings.summary: A three-task smoke screen checks new verification evidence and process cleanup on the adopted assembly. Targeted contracts pass. Ordinary task outcomes cannot validate exceptional timeout paths that do not occur in the screen.

findings.title: A coherent component update remains unqualified
findings.summary: All nine full-pipeline attempts finished on the committed component set. One produced a valid Intent and landed with review approval, but none passed every hidden check. Three additional shape-only attempts produced no Intent. The registered comparison changes classification when historical approval timeouts are excluded, and a readiness harm guard also fires. The set remains unqualified; the reproduction pack retains all outcomes and both readings.

findings.title: A coherent component update regresses task readiness
findings.summary: Candidate-only Terra medium screen of the current coherent component mains: 2/9 valid Intents, 2/9 landed, 0/9 hidden all-passes. Registered reading: WORSE. Task-level harms and both timeout sensitivities remain visible. No individual component effect is claimed.

findings.title: A bounded follow-up leaves the component update unqualified
findings.summary: Two follow-up attempts produced one valid Intent and one landed change, but neither passed every hidden check. A generated acceptance contract had undefined steps, triggering the registered stop before a third launch. Both historical-timeout readings retain a readiness harm. The original screen and every harm remain in the pack; no component is qualified and the confirmation is closed without adoption.

findings.title: Verification caller cancellation follow-up
findings.summary: All three task attempts were graded. One landed and two stopped in shaping; no natural caller-cancellation event occurred, so efficacy remains unresolved.

findings.title: Coordinator validation feedback screen
findings.summary: All three candidate tasks and their stored comparisons failed whole-task hidden grading. Changed validation feedback was not observed; the component remains unresolved.

findings.title: Retained verification diagnostics and repair locations
findings.summary: A model-free replay preserves failure symptoms but does not establish tested revisions or faster repairs. The proposed model comparison remains incomplete.

findings.title: Shaping repair paired screen
findings.summary: Across nine graded paired tasks, neither build achieved whole-task hidden all-pass; the candidate lost valid Intent on two targeted tasks while improving one held-out result. Two pairs remained unrun and acceptance separation could not be measured.

findings.title: Shaping repair completed paired screen
findings.summary: All eleven pairs completed. Control had 6 valid Intents and 2 landings; candidate had 4 and 4. The owner rule says keep. Acceptance separation remains unknown.

findings.title: A readiness regression claim remains tentative after targeted repeats
findings.summary: A bounded recheck of two coherent component versions keeps earlier readiness-regression claims tentative. Intent validity, generated acceptance, final hidden correctness and environment stops are reported separately. No harmful component commit is established, and useful checks remain intact.

findings.title: Three-task Loop evidence wave
findings.summary: Three request-only tasks examined on the current release; no new Loop fault demonstrated. Two stopped for questions. No valid matched behavior comparison; tool feedback coverage is incomplete.

findings.title: Saved-candidate reviews after four changes
findings.summary: A completed 36-review screen detects 4 versus 3 held-out target mechanisms. Repair verification and the clean-control result remain unresolved, so no improvement is qualified.

findings.title: Repair after shaping refusals remains tentative
findings.summary: A bounded repair window led to two saved Intents on nine assignments, compared with one in each of two stored draws. None passed all hidden checks, and some question handoffs became refusals. The small screen is unresolved.

findings.title: Build head paired screen remains tentative
findings.summary: Four paired tasks included one tentative candidate-worse smoke outcome that occurred before Build; both guard arms landed but neither passed all hidden checks. The component's effect remains unresolved. Original cell traces were inadvertently deleted after summary extraction.

findings.title: Bounded shaping recovery confirmation
findings.summary: A confirmation stopped after two invalid-submission failures. Neither saved an Intent, and the improvement remains unresolved; one assignment ran out of order.

findings.title: Build component head with a fixed Intent
findings.summary: This tentative four-task paired screen compares the current build component with the release. The sample is too small to establish an improvement or regression.

findings.title: Review component head with a fixed Intent
findings.summary: The candidate scored lower on this four-task screen; the result is tentative because the sample is small and several hidden checks errored.

findings.title: Review head regression not confirmed
findings.summary: Across four original tasks and one held-out task, two repetitions each, the release and the release with the newer review component passed exactly the same hidden checks in all 20 cells (50 of 98 per arm). The earlier regression signal was not reproduced, so no revert is requested.

findings.title: Context packet did not speed up four tasks
findings.summary: In a matched screen of four public coding tasks, two repetitions each, every cell passed in both arms. Agents given an automatic Kogen Context packet were not faster (median 46.0 s against 43.6 s) and used 23% more uncached input tokens. On both Rust tasks the packet missed the file the agent edited, and an earlier speedup on one of them did not replicate. Unresolved.

findings.title: Review component on Claude: no difference attributable (tentative)
findings.summary: On Claude Sonnet 5.5 with frozen Intents, the release and the release with the newer review component landed the same four paired tasks and passed 24 and 25 of 34 hidden checks. Review approved every cell and no difference traces to review; one attempt per task is only a smoke test.

findings.title: Build main head on Claude: no clear difference (tentative)
findings.summary: On Claude Sonnet 5.5 with frozen Intents, the release and the release with the build main head both landed all five tasks and passed 40 and 38 of 49 hidden checks. The one lower task is inside the release's own spread on that task; one attempt per task is only a smoke test.

findings.title: Message Batches review of landed commits
findings.summary: The Message Batches API reviewed 93 landed commits for half the synchronous price, but a first pass cut 37 reviews short and the comparison with the seat-run review is weak, so the result is unresolved.

findings.title: What keeps the prompt cache warm (unconfirmed probe)
findings.summary: In an 11-call probe, a cached prefix was reused after effort changes and with thinking omitted, but not when thinking was set to between_tools or when the model changed. It is one prefix and one run, so it is an unconfirmed probe and the result is unresolved.

findings.title: Packet-only localization over the API
findings.summary: With the Kogen Context packet a no-tools model named the right first file in all 7 scored calls versus 4 of 8 without it. It is a small pilot of localization only, so the result is unresolved.

findings.title: Shaping recovery on Claude: one rescue, otherwise a tie (tentative)
findings.summary: On Claude Sonnet 5.5 request-only, the release with bounded refusal recovery produced 5 of 7 valid Intents against 4 of 7 and passed all hidden checks on 3 tasks against 2. The mechanism rescued one refused shaping, whose Build then blocked; one attempt per task is only a smoke test.

findings.title: Packet-only localization on 11 more cases
findings.summary: On 11 fresh cases in four languages, a no-tools model named the right source file just as often with the Kogen Context packet as without it (identical in all 11 cases), at 1.9 times the input tokens. The issue text alone already names the file in 10 of 11 cases, so this cheap check cannot show a gain; it is a pre-screen for the build screen and says nothing about verified outcomes.

findings.title: Build component check on Claude stays unresolved
findings.summary: Both arms ran the same Claude model on four supplied-Intent tasks. Two cells stopped before building because an approval step timed out on a loaded machine, so only two tasks form valid pairs: the Go task passed in full in both arms, and on the deployment task the candidate failed one more hidden check than the release. A single flip is within normal repeat variation, so there is no attributable regression and no gain.

findings.title: Review component check on Claude stays unresolved
findings.summary: Both arms ran the same Claude model on four supplied-Intent tasks. Two tasks never got past an approval step that timed out on a loaded machine, so only two tasks form valid pairs. The Go task passed in full in both arms and the deployment task scored the same low result in both, with the review stage approving both. There is no difference between arms, so no regression and no gain can be shown.

findings.title: Shaping recovery on Claude: second smoke run, unresolved
findings.summary: With both arms on one Claude model, the bounded refusal-recovery change turned one refused shaping into a valid Intent and failed to rescue another. Hidden checks favoured the release (19 of 40 against 7 of 40), but that gap comes from build-stage timeouts and different Intents, not the patched stage. Two tasks had no pair after a provider limit stopped them, and one attempt per task is only a smoke test.

findings.title: Context packet shows no time-to-patch gain in a screen
findings.summary: In 10 matched pairs on five real tasks (three in Zig, two in Rust), the agent produced a patch that passed the hidden check in every run with and without the Kogen Context packet. The median time ratio was 1.02 on Zig and 1.00 on Rust, so the claimed shortening did not appear. Most runs ended at the 300 second cap with the fix already made, so the times mostly measure the cap. This is a screen with one model, not a speed claim.

findings.title: A brief marker did not detect compaction; the hook did
findings.summary: A marker echoed on every call caught 0 of 26 forced compactions, because the compaction summary repeats it word for word; the client's SessionStart hook caught 52 of 52. The marker costs about 6 tokens per call with no false alarms, but it fails the detection test, so it is not adopted. Short headless sessions with forced compaction were tested; the Codex client was not.

findings.title: Hook-free compaction detection: markers fail, a self-check works, the hook needs the launcher
findings.summary: Values held in context (a content hash, a nonce, a rotating receipt) caught 0 of 8 forced compactions each, because the compaction summary copies them. A self-check where the agent reports whether it still holds the brief word for word caught 31 of 31 losses with no false alarm in 90 calls, at about 6 tokens per call. A hook the agent installs fired on 29 of 29 compactions when the client allowed the write, but the write was refused 9 of 9 times in the default permission mode, so the launcher has to install it. The recommended brief text recovered the brief after 22 of 22 compactions. The result is mixed by design: Claude Code in short headless sessions only, Codex not run.

findings.title: Alarm relays to main: one line per event removes every repeat
findings.summary: Replaying 4.8 days of recorded alarms, 57% of the 1,092 lines relayed to the main session repeated an event already relayed. Delivering one line per event removes all repeats and cuts relay messages by 31% without delaying or dropping a first alarm. Adding escalation to the next role adds 523 messages and pages the project owner 51 times a day, because nobody acknowledged an alarm in that period; leases have nothing to remove because one process launches all work. The fix addresses about a quarter of main's traffic, not the 91% quoted for it.

findings.title: Slow checks re-run on an unchanged tree: little to save, and already shipped
findings.summary: In 101 stored Kogen Builds, a check of 60 s or more repeated on an identical tree in 12 Builds, 2.75% of total Build wall, always the re-verify after review approval; kogen-build already reuses a green check per tree since 3 Nov, so the queued opt-in reuse is not built. Reusing a baseline across restarted Builds saved 3.6% of wall on a surrogate key and could not be checked, because no stored log carries run identity.

findings.title: Handoff questions stopped shaping before the question check, not after
findings.summary: In 626 shaping runs, 11 stopped on an authentication or security handoff question (1.76 per 100). All 11 ran before the question check landed; 0 of 197 runs after it did, and none of 80 questions in 549 stored research cells was classed as a handoff. No handoff was clearly one only the user could answer, so an evidence gate on handoffs is not built. One question in 81 had no options and no recommended answer and still passes today, so only that check is built.

findings.title: Changed-first checks in build rounds: the targeted test run is not cheap enough
findings.summary: On the frozen start trees of four slow-suite tasks, the targeted form of a heavy check (only tests tied to the changed files) cost 0.02, 0.23 and 0.69 of the full mix test, and for one task no test maps to the change; the registered gate needed 3 of 4 at half the full cost or less and got 2, so arm A2 gets no cells and the row closes as measured. Model-free timing on a loaded host; whether the targeted form misses failures the full run catches was not measured.

findings.title: Sharing a source copy does not cut MacBook temp-file load
findings.summary: One Build on the MacBook created 1.72 million temp files in 23 minutes, none from the four suspected sources; a shared source copy could remove at most 2.8% of the largest test's files. The load is the release package's npm files, rebuilt and re-extracted per test; sharing them cut files 50% to 97% and file-event CPU 22% to 66% with every test passing, but those versions change 11 links in the package, so no fix is proven yet.

findings.title: Linux check helper leaves zombies; reaping while the check runs fixes it in a first run
findings.summary: Kogen's Linux check helper waits only for its shell, so a process killed during a check stays a zombie until the check ends. A test that kills a process group and waits for it then hangs. With the released helper, the kogen-shaping test suite failed at its 10-minute timeout with the same two tests as the failed Builds, and a kill-group probe saw the killed process as a zombie for 5 seconds in 2 of 2 runs. A helper that reaps every exited child while the check runs passed every run: the suite ran in 210.5 s against 217.9 s with no helper, and it still stopped all four detached servers that survive without a helper. This is tentative: one Linux host and part of one repetition ran, because delivery Builds took the host, so B ran 2 of the 30 suite runs the rule needs.

findings.title: Static checks on shaped files stop 1 of 22 defects the builder refuses
findings.summary: The repository's own format, vet and syntax checks, run on shaper-written acceptance files before approve, caught 1 of 22 builder-blocked defects (a Go driver that was not gofmt-formatted). With the 6 readiness refusals that already happen, 7 of 28 failures are stopped. The rest are semantic: contradictory steps, wrong expected values, fixtures that do not match the code, timing, string escaping. No false refusals in 30 landed Intents, and 1 in 12 in-scope Go packages. Shaped bytes survived for only 5 of the 28 failures, the rest were scored from logs and probes. The 60% bar is not met, so the shape-repair comparison is needed.

findings.title: A probe copy with git history lets git-reading observers pass
findings.summary: Readiness runs observers in a scratch copy without git metadata, so an observer that reads git fails. Giving the copy a shared clone of the source at its HEAD, with hooks off, made 6 of 6 feasibility commands of the 3 affected Intents pass (0 of 6 before) and left 10 git-free controls unchanged in all 20 commands; a probe that writes config, files and a commit leaves the source untouched. The three observers are reconstructions and the replay stops at the probe, not a full approve. A request for the verification component is filed.

findings.title: Detecting compaction without a model: a transcript watcher always works, token drop only on long sessions
findings.summary: A process that reads the harness transcript caught all 173 forced compactions in the earlier short test sessions, and all 129 Claude Code and 165 Codex compactions in real long sessions; on real sessions that rate holds by construction, because it reads the same entries that define the truth. A detector that looks for a large fall in context size caught none of the 173 in the short sessions, where the fixed prompt dominates, but all 129 and 165 in real sessions, with about 0.002 false alarms per 100 calls. Neither needs a model call, and both can act only at the agent's next call to the service, which also needs the loop id from the launcher. The real-session corpus is private, so only counts are published. Whether a new-nonce instruction helps is a separate, later test.

findings.title: Extracting one release file cuts the biggest MacBook test's temp files by 46%
findings.summary: The release-assembly test unpacked the whole release package (about 7,500 files) to read one executable. Extracting only that executable cut the files it creates per run by 46% (15,425 to 8,297) and file-event CPU in 7 of 8 paired rounds, with every test passing and the package unchanged, so a change request is filed.

findings.title: Batching Kogen's approval step-binding check cuts approval time by over 90%
findings.summary: Since release 41d70052, approving an Intent starts one Node and Cucumber process per step text for every pair of step files with every earlier Intent, so approval grows with the repository's history; the delivery launcher also approves twice per Build. On frozen copies of real shaped trees, with no language model involved, a Lab build that loads each pair of step files once and matches all step texts in that process cut approval time by 91.9-96.3% on all 7 trees (pooled 16,360 s to 1,093 s; Studio trees about 50 minutes to 4). It reached the same step-binding verdict as the release on 12 of 12 fixtures and refused all 3 synthetic collisions with identical text. The three final-verdict differences were readiness timeouts under host load, a stage the change does not touch. Calling approve once instead of twice saved only -10% to 57% and needs a digest the launcher does not have, so it was not adopted.

findings.title: Shared Go lock for small suites stays unresolved
findings.summary: The replay of four parallel Build streams under an exclusive, a shared-small and a capped shared lock could not run because the only allowed Linux host was never quiet: 2.8% of monitored samples passed the guard and the longest quiet stretch was 20 seconds. A trace-driven estimate from the 48-hour lock logs says sharing only small suites removes under a third of lock wait, and sharing large suites removes most of it but barely changes total wait plus run time if large suites slow down 2x. False-red risk is not estimable without the replay.

findings.title: Verify timeouts and land-red under load stay unresolved
findings.summary: No failing tree was re-run solo and under load: no quiet host was available and the original trees were deleted. Retained logs show all 10 host-or-base Builds ended at the default 10-minute go test timeout, three of them in the same kogen-verification test, while none of the 28 land-red retries mention a timeout and most show deterministic assertion or compile failures. No fix is chosen from log text alone.

findings.title: Reading a Build's final outcome fixes delivery's misreads
findings.summary: Over the 157 failed Kogen Builds of 2-5 Nov, delivery's old first-line read of the log agreed with the hand-assigned real outcome in 107 cases (68%) and recorded 3 of the 4 green Builds as failed. A reader of the final outcome agrees in 156 (99.4%), reads every green Build as green (also 472 further landed Builds) and no failed Build as green. Delivery's own interim fix of 5 Nov already reaches 153; the reader adds the 'already present' Builds, a Build killed during approval, and a lost exit line after a terminated launch wrapper. The rules were fitted on the same logs and the hand truth has no second labeller.

findings.title: An allow-list for the budget-off consumer test: not measured
findings.summary: The measured comparison of the budget-off test against an allow-list projection did not run: none of 260 checks of the two allowed Linux hosts found them quiet, so there is no false-red rate and no mutation result. A host-free replay of the four keys behind the recorded reds shows all four were red under the deny-list of their own window and one still is today, while the allow-list compares none of them and keeps any budget field. That is a design check, not a measurement, so the question stays open.

findings.title: Isolated, parallel-safe generated acceptance: no detector with a payoff passes
findings.summary: Tested three detectors on Kogen's own 604-scenario acceptance with 14 seeded hazards run and 40 scanned. A static lint refuses none of 509 real files but the real corpus holds no port or path hazard; a measured-wall check falsely refuses 10 of 28 sampled Intents at 10 s; two concurrent shuffled copies catch collisions when they overlap but add a median 14% wall. The first full suite run was stopped at 81 minutes and delivery Builds shared the host, so the numbers are a sample.

findings.title: kogen-loop is faster and lighter than Claude Code on the same API key
findings.summary: Same model (claude-sonnet-5-5, medium effort), prompt, server and API key, 12 Go tasks x 2 repetitions. kogen-loop took 0.80x the agent wall time of Claude Code configured as Kogen runs it and 0.88x that of a lean Claude Code, faster in 21 of 23 paired blocks each, with 0.64x and 0.85x the tokens and 2-3 fewer requests per task. Passes: loop 21/24, Kogen-style Claude Code 20/23, lean 22/23. Kogen's executor arguments cost Claude Code about 9% wall and 33% tokens; running Claude Code with kogen-loop's instructions as its system prompt was no slower and passed 24/24. Descriptive; the last block's two Claude Code cells did not run (spend cap).

findings.title: The wall-time deadline test starts its clock too early; the loaded run did not happen
findings.summary: A kogen-verification test gives a whole verification call 300 ms and then expects its first setup command to have run 100 ms. In 300 of 300 probe runs on a busy Mac the call spent 215-297 ms before that command even started. The unchanged test failed 2 of 600 runs (both: the command never started); a variant whose clock starts at the command failed 0 of 600, and a mutant that ignores the deadline still fails it. The planned loaded Linux run could not take its host lock, so the rate delivery saw at higher load was not reproduced here. The variant was adopted under a recorded deviation: the land checks' own failures at high load stand in for the loaded run.

findings.title: On Linux the wall-time deadline test does not fail; its pre-setup work is 4x shorter than on the Mac
findings.summary: The Linux leg of the wall-time deadline test Lab. On a 4-core server the unchanged kogen-verification test passed 600 of 600 runs, quiet and under a fixed background build load, and so did the variant whose 300 ms clock starts at the first setup command. A probe shows why: there the verification call spends 23-77 ms before that command starts, against 215-297 ms on the Mac where the test failed. The test's fixed budget is tight only where the work before setup is slow. By the registered rule the Linux reproduction failed; with the Mac evidence the variant was adopted under a recorded deviation.

findings.title: Unconditional kogen check at landing fails its rule: it refuses good commits and reproduces 1 of 8 breakers
findings.summary: Replaying 48 component landings (8 breakers, 40 known-good) with kogen's go build, vet and test run on the landing-time kogen main after pinning the landed commit: the registered rule fails (12 of 31 good commits refused, limit 2). Strict recall looks high (7 of 8) but only 1 breaker is refused for the reported reason; the rest are refused by a hard-coded-pin test fixed in kogen on 4 Nov or by loop-module skew, and some are not reproduced at all. Good commits are also refused for coupling between components and for kogen tests that kogen edited with the move. About 4.8 minutes added per landing. Not built as specified; the tuple variant refuses good commits too, because kogen's tests lag legitimate component moves.

findings.title: No review arm of the wide-change Lab passes Stage 0; today's review already cuts 9 parts to 3
findings.summary: Replaying the K-MODELS-FILE review requests with no model: current review cuts the 9-part, 4,142,106-byte sequence to 3 parts and 1,403,877 bytes, but stops on 4,000 tiny paths because the repeated catalog exceeds the ceiling. Of the registered arms, a digest per part (R1) fails the same way, on-demand reads (R2) grow quadratically, and a path-and-status catalog (R3) sends but costs 9.644x. Token and dollar figures are estimates from one logged Build; no review quality was measured.

findings.title: A new-nonce instruction detected 8 of 8 forced compactions in a small Claude Code test
findings.summary: Telling the agent to invent a new nonce after its context is compacted, and checking at its next call to the service that the value changed, detected 8 of 8 forced compactions and raised no false alarm in 36 other calls; the compaction hook caught the same 8. The earlier static nonce caught 0 of 8 because the summary copies the value. The result is tentative: 8 compactions, short headless sessions, one model and client version, forced compaction only. It shows that the agent noticed the compaction, not that the whole brief survived, it depends on the model obeying the instruction, and the service can only react at the next call. Codex was not run.

findings.title: A behaviour projection leaves every recorded false red of the budget-off test outside it
findings.summary: Of the 14 land windows where kogen-build's budget-off test went red, 13 could be identified and 10 record the differing key: request timing, host load, a sweep duration and a toolchain-probe status, none of them an exit code, stop reason, commit fact, request count or budget field. A behaviour projection would not have gone red for any of them, and a planted budget key is inside it. This is step 0 with no run; whether the projection still catches real defects is step 1 (Lab C6, unmeasured).

findings.title: The tests request's time budgets cannot yet be priced from recorded logs
findings.summary: From 48 hours of recorded suite logs, 6 of 15 repo-by-host rows already meet the request's time budgets and 9 do not. Only kogen's packaging and builds (81 s) have a recorded cost; the 130 s and 120 s waits the request moves to the release tier already run in parallel, so moving them lowers a floor but not the wall, and the remaining gaps (kogen-build 271 s, kogen-shaping 76 s, kogen 110 s on the MacBook) need a per-test profile. Parallelism alone reaches the budget for coordinator, setup and verification but not for shaping on Linux.

findings.title: The replay's Quint batch is fast, but its generator rejects 7 of 17 valid acceptance runs
findings.summary: Kogen's existing conformance replay stops at its first journey on the current main for five independent reasons. Recording 17 passing acceptance Builds and replaying them in one Quint file takes about 2 seconds, well inside 10, but 7 of the 17 are rejected because the trace generator does not map a baseline change, a reviewer repair or a hook-changed commit to the model's actions. Only 9 of the 36 model-tagged scenarios can be replayed by the existing build-model generator; 20 have no generator.

findings.title: Archiving per-Intent step files leaves the spec trace unchanged, but many of them already name tests that no longer exist
findings.summary: Of 289 per-Intent step files that run go test, 220 name tests; 29 of those name tests that exist nowhere today (one still runs a test removed with the experimental levers) and 69 cannot be mapped to a test name. Moving 99 of kogen's step files leaves the specification trace byte-identical, so no requirement loses its scenario. The registered bar fails because of the stale observers, which nothing runs; they need a one-time clean-up before the archive move.

findings.title: A model-free scope inventory names every owner-keyed store the hidden checks touch; the counted shaper cells were not run
findings.summary: Scored by a judge who did not write the scanner, the stored inventories of 13 application start trees name all 106 owner-keyed tables that the hidden checks touch (recall 1.00 on 13 of 13 trees, 0.94 mean over all 121 touched tables; the 14 misses are identity, session and one-hop join tables). One dry cell per arm (inventory in the first message, inventory as an answered tool call, review-side only) put both known stores into a saved Intent or draft. The 18 counted cells did not start because the only open seat was refused by admission, so the target gate (stores named in 4 of 6 valid Intents) and the guard bar are unmeasured and no arm is proven.

findings.title: Reaping while the check runs ends the Linux helper's hangs, with no orphans
findings.summary: Kogen's Linux check helper leaves a process that exits during a check as a zombie, so a test that kills a process group and waits for it hangs to its 10 minute timeout. Over 10 repetitions on one Linux host, the released helper failed kogen-shaping and kogen-loop's go-test check in all 20 runs, every time at the timeout, and a kill-group probe failed 10 of 10. A helper that reaps every exited child while the check runs passed all 30 go-test runs (within 3 percent of no helper on every repository, kogen-loop unchanged) with no orphans, and still stopped all detached servers, which no-helper leaves. The registered failure clause is read over the two repositories that have such a test (kogen-verification has none).

findings.title: A refused review submission should not make its requirement texts binding
findings.summary: An independent review of kogen-review kept the requirement texts of every submission, refused ones included, as binding, and allowed one refusal. A reviewer refused once for an evidence problem who then split or reworded its requirements was refused again only because the first wording was missing, and the review ended without a verdict. Replaying the 5 recorded sequences of 3 failed Builds through the real review path, the unchanged code ended invalid on 5 of 5 (and reproduced the logged counts exactly) while listing texts only from accepted submissions approved 5 of 5, including a round that restored 23 accepted texts. A drop of an accepted requirement is still refused, and the Go suite stays green once the one test that asserted the old rule is updated. First-round refusal causes are the replay's reading; no native-reviewer sequence was recorded.

findings.title: The decision-record gate costs one shaping attempt, but other gates end these shapes before readiness
findings.summary: Four shapes ended with readiness 0.0 s after kogen-shaping's decision-record gate refused attempt 1 on every tree (7 problems: 4 command text, 2 URLs, 1 file the same package proposes, none a missing file). None ended on that gate's citation check; the endings were a decision check, a revises text, the review-size bound and the carried-decisions check. A small change that notes such sources as unverified lets all four attempt-1 decisions through, still refuses a real missing file and adds no test failure, but the same packages then stop at the size bound (3 trees, 1.18 to 1.35 MB against 524,288 bytes) or the carried-decisions check (1 tree), so readiness still runs on 0 of 4. Without a model, what a shaper does with the extra attempt is not tested.

findings.title: The review-size bound counts whole files the review never carries, and the one change that passes it removes the gate
findings.summary: After the decision-record change, shaping stopped at the review-size bound on three of four recorded shapes: the estimate was 1.18 to 1.35 MB against 524,288 bytes. The Intent package itself is 87 to 140 KB (7 to 10%). The rest is the size at HEAD of every file the Intent names in backticks, changed or not, and one generated data file of 597,140 bytes is 44 to 50% on its own; repeated lines are under 0.3%. The review stage uses the same constant but its prompt holds only the Intent, feature, model, check results, diffs and added files, and it reviews a larger source in parts instead of refusing. Counting the generated file and repeats once leaves all three trees 12 to 43% over. A one-line change that stops summing named files lets the gate pass on 3 of 3 trees and still refuses a package whose own text is over the bound, but it fails 4 of the delivered scope tests, such a package already ends shaping at the shaper's context window, and readiness still runs on 0 of 4 (the next gate is the carried-decisions check). The rule (no new suite failure) is not met, so no change is requested; whether the gate stays as a cost guard is a design decision. No model was used; a real shaper's next attempt and a Build's real review size are untested.

findings.title: On macOS, Go tests started detached are scanned by XProtect; attached to ssh they are not
findings.summary: On a macOS build host, a Go test started the way delivery starts Builds (over ssh with nohup, reparented to launchd) made the XProtect scanner spend 1.35 to 1.39 s of CPU per run of a 10-package test, and the same command attached to an ssh session spent 0.00 s in every run (3 against 3; one package: 2 against 2). The detached run also took about 8 percent longer. At that scale the scanner uses about 10 percent of a core while the test runs; a Build's much larger suite reaches the roughly 40 percent seen during Builds by the same mechanism, which was not run. One host, one repository.

findings.title: Request-only shaping refusals are mostly prompt-versus-gate contradictions, and gate-side changes alone turn 2 of 5
findings.summary: In the first block of a smoke round, kogen-shaping's own gates refused all five Kogen shapes on request-only Rails tasks, three submissions each, so every Kogen cell scored the start-tree floor. Replaying the 13 recorded refusals through the package's gate functions reproduced every recorded count. Of 89 problem lines, 60 ask for something the shaper prompt never names (the assumption and evidence forms, observer files in the Intent folder), 15 are shaper errors and 14 are prose statements with no named way to mark them. Three small gate-side changes keep all 19 negative cases refused and accept every stored Intent the pinned code accepts (415 of 415), but together turn only 2 of the 5 first refusals into passes (the two that wrote observer files into the Intent folder), against a registered need of 4. The rest need the shaper to mark or format what it writes, which is a prompt change that has to be measured with a model. No model call.

findings.title: The shaper prompt change gets one of five refused tasks to readiness; the rest stop at prose statements and later gates
findings.summary: Stage 0 found that most refusal lines of five request-only Rails shapes were a contradiction between the shaper prompt and a gate, and that gate-side changes alone turn 2 of 5 first refusals. This screen runs the prompt change with those gate changes on a model (Claude Code, Sonnet 5.5, high effort, shape only, request only, no answerer). Only 6 of 30 planned cells ran, because the subscription seat's pace limit held new cells: 1 release cell and 5 candidate cells, one per refused task. The candidate reached readiness on 1 of 5 (the release: 0 of 1, and 0 of 5 in the earlier round); the rule needs 7 of 10, so it fails on its first check even if every unrun candidate cell had passed (at most 6 of 10). The new markers were used (10 to 15 per Intent against 7) and decision-check lines fell, but prose statements without a marker still stopped two tasks, and three of four refused candidate cells ended at gates the release never reached (readiness controls, contract review). The held-out tasks were not run, so that check was not evaluated; no request is made.

findings.title: The second shaper text changes leave all six cells at the 30-minute deadline, with the first draft using most of it
findings.summary: Stage 1 reached readiness on 1 of 5 refused tasks, and its refusals were classified model-free. A second set of general text changes (P2, then P2b) was screened on a model (Claude Code, Sonnet 5.5, high effort, shape only, request only, no answerer). Only 6 of 24 planned cells ran, and none reached readiness: all six ended at the 1800 s shape deadline, which is Kogen's own shape budget. The first shaper round alone took 1209 to 1800 s against 410 to 1019 s for stage 1's candidate cells, so the cells ran out of time before they ran out of attempts. The text changes did move the refusals down the gate chain: the decision check refused once in 6 cells (stage 1: 8 refusals in 5 cells), two cells reached the last gate before readiness, and one was past four gates with no refusal when time ran out. P2 told the shaper to list every observer file under Acceptance, which the step-ownership gate refuses, so it sent the shaper into a new refusal class; P2b corrected it and none of its three cells met that class. By the registered rule the verdict is unresolved (6 of the 20 cells needed), not no: three failures leave the 7 of 10 requirement possible. Held-out tasks and the release control were not run. Stage 3 should use P2b and report first-round time next to readiness.

findings.title: Naming the gate forms in the shaper prompt gets small requests through shaping; the Rails tasks stop at later gates
findings.summary: The release, shaping ordinary small requests with nothing but the request (a new function, a validation rule, a CLI flag, a rename, a bug fix over small Python, Go and Node repositories), reached readiness on 3 of 25 cells and never at the first attempt: its own gates refused the forms its shaper prompt had asked for. Six rounds of small, general changes (prompt text that names the assumption and evidence markers, keeps repository facts and examples out of the Intent text and states the step and Tests forms, plus one sentence in the decision checker's instructions and stage 1's three gate changes) reached readiness on 10 of 10 climb requests and, on five held-out requests run twice, on 10 of 10 cells, 8 at the first attempt, against the release's 2 of 10. The same changes on the five request-only Rails tasks the release was refused on reached readiness on 0 of 5: the shapes passed the gates that stopped the release and stopped at later ones (the wrong-implementation controls file no prompt names, the decision record refusing probe runs cited as evidence, dropped earlier decisions), two at the 30-minute deadline. The rule needed 2 of 5, so the verdict is no and no request is made from this stage; gate negative cases and the package's test suite are unchanged.
